people/ann-lee/summary: English-born leader of the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing (Shakers), whom her followers regarded as the female embodiment of the Christ Spirit; taught celibacy, confession and ecstatic worship. Shaker theology lies outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
people/ann-lee/keyIdeas/0: Celibacy as the way of salvation
people/ann-lee/keyIdeas/2: Christ's second appearing in female form (Shaker belief)
people/james-mcquilkin/summary: Ulster Presbyterian layman whose prayer meeting near Kells, Co. Antrim, begun in 1857, is regarded as the starting point of the Ulster Revival of 1859.
people/maria-woodworth-etter/summary: American Holiness and later Pentecostal evangelist known for large tent meetings marked by 'trances' and healing claims from the 1880s, and for the Dallas campaign of 1912.
people/maria-woodworth-etter/keyIdeas/2: Power of the Spirit in revival
people/willis-hoover/summary: American Methodist missionary in Chile whose Valparaíso congregation experienced a Pentecostal revival in 1909; after his break with the Methodist conference he led the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal (1910).
people/marie-monsen/summary: Norwegian Lutheran missionary in China (from 1901) whose searching preaching on the new birth helped spark the Shantung Revival of 1927-1937.
people/marie-monsen/keyIdeas/0: The necessity of the new birth
people/duncan-campbell/summary: Scottish Faith Mission evangelist associated with the Lewis (Hebrides) Awakening of 1949-1952, later principal of the Faith Mission Bible College in Edinburgh.
people/duncan-campbell/keyIdeas/1: Holiness and the presence of God
people/agnes-sasagawa/summary: Japanese Catholic sister of the Handmaids of the Eucharist at Akita, who reported the messages and phenomena associated with Our Lady of Akita (1973-1981), recognised by her bishop in 1984.
people/alphonsine-mumureke/summary: Rwandan Catholic who as a student at Kibeho College reported the first apparition of the Virgin Mary as 'Nyina wa Jambo' (28 November 1981); one of three visionaries whose apparitions were approved in 2001.
people/paul-of-tarsus/summary: A Pharisee from Tarsus who persecuted the early church until a vision of the risen Christ made him 'apostle to the Gentiles'. His missionary journeys planted churches across Asia Minor and Greece, and his letters — the earliest Christian writings — shaped all later theology of grace, faith, the Law and the church. Tradition holds he was beheaded in Rome under Nero.
people/paul-of-tarsus/keyIdeas/0: Justification by faith apart from works of the Law
people/paul-of-tarsus/keyIdeas/1: Gentiles included in God's people without circumcision
people/paul-of-tarsus/keyIdeas/2: The church as the body of Christ
people/peter-apostle/summary: A Galilean fisherman, leader of the Twelve and first preacher at Pentecost according to Acts. He led the Jerusalem community, accepted Gentiles at Cornelius's house and, by strong early tradition, was martyred in Rome under Nero. Catholics regard him as the first pope; others honour him as chief apostle without accepting papal claims derived from him.
people/peter-apostle/keyIdeas/1: Leadership of the early Jerusalem church
people/james-of-jerusalem/summary: Called 'the brother of the Lord', James became leader of the Jerusalem church and presided at the council of Jerusalem. Known as 'the Just' for his Torah piety, he was stoned in 62 according to Josephus. The Letter of James is traditionally attributed to him.
people/john-apostle/summary: Son of Zebedee and one of the inner circle of the Twelve. Tradition identifies him with the Beloved Disciple and the author of the Fourth Gospel, three letters and Revelation, and places his old age at Ephesus. Modern scholars debate these attributions.
people/john-apostle/keyIdeas/2: Eternal life now through knowing Christ
people/thomas-apostle/summary: One of the Twelve, remembered in John's Gospel for doubting and then confessing 'My Lord and my God'. Strong tradition, recorded in the Acts of Thomas and cherished by Kerala's Christians, holds that he evangelised Parthia and India, arriving in 52 and dying as a martyr at Mylapore around 72.
people/clement-of-rome/summary: Leader of the Roman church at the end of the first century, listed by Irenaeus as the third successor of Peter. His letter to the Corinthians (c. 96) urges order and humility and is the earliest Christian text outside the New Testament.
people/ignatius-of-antioch/summary: Bishop of Antioch who, under guard on his way to martyrdom in Rome, wrote seven letters to churches. He stressed the unity of the church around the bishop, the real flesh of Christ against docetism, and the Eucharist; he is the first to use the phrase 'catholic church'.
people/polycarp/summary: Bishop of Smyrna who, according to Irenaeus, had known the apostle John. He wrote a letter to the Philippians and was burned at about 86 years old after refusing to curse Christ. The account of his death is the earliest martyr-act.
people/justin-martyr/summary: Born in Samaria, Justin searched among the philosophical schools before conversion, then taught Christianity as the true philosophy in Rome. His Apologies and Dialogue with Trypho present Christ as the Logos who sowed seeds of truth among all peoples. He was beheaded around 165.
people/marcion/summary: A wealthy shipowner who taught in Rome that the God of Israel was a just but lesser creator distinct from the good Father revealed by Jesus. Excommunicated around 144, he founded churches with his own canon of edited Luke and Pauline letters, provoking the wider church to define its Scriptures.
people/marcion/keyIdeas/0: Two Gods: just creator and good Father
people/irenaeus/summary: Born in Smyrna, where as a youth he heard Polycarp, Irenaeus became bishop of Lyon after the persecution of 177. His Against Heresies refuted Valentinian Gnosticism by appeal to the apostolic rule of faith, the four Gospels and the succession of bishops, and his Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching summarises the faith. He taught that Christ 'recapitulates' humanity, reversing Adam's disobedience.
people/irenaeus/keyIdeas/1: Rule of faith and apostolic succession
people/irenaeus/keyIdeas/3: Goodness of creation against Gnostic dualism
people/montanus/summary: A recent convert in Phrygia (fl. c. 156–172) who, with the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, uttered ecstatic oracles as the mouthpiece of the Paraclete. The 'New Prophecy' urged strict fasting and readiness for martyrdom and expected the heavenly Jerusalem to descend at Pepouza.
people/tertullian/summary: A brilliant and combative Carthaginian writer, the first major Christian author in Latin. He coined much of the West's Trinitarian vocabulary — trinitas, one substance in three persons — and wrote against Marcion and Praxeas; later in life he sympathised with the Montanist New Prophecy.
people/perpetua/summary: A 22-year-old noblewoman and new mother of Carthage, martyred with her slave Felicity and fellow catechumens in the arena. Her prison diary, recording visions of a ladder to heaven and of combat with the devil, is among the earliest texts by a Christian woman.
people/clement-of-alexandria/summary: An Athenian-educated convert who led the catechetical school at Alexandria. In the Exhortation, Instructor and Miscellanies he presented Christ as the divine Teacher and Christianity as the fulfilment of Greek philosophy, describing the mature believer as the true 'gnostic'.
people/clement-of-alexandria/keyIdeas/0: Philosophy as preparation for the gospel
people/origen/summary: The most prolific scholar of the early church, head of the Alexandrian school and later teacher at Caesarea. His Hexapla, commentaries and On First Principles pioneered textual criticism and spiritual exegesis. Tortured in the Decian persecution, he died soon after; some speculations (pre-existence of souls, universal restoration) were condemned in 553.
people/cyprian/summary: A wealthy rhetor converted in middle age who became bishop of Carthage. During the Decian persecution he led from hiding and then addressed the reconciliation of the lapsed; his treatise On the Unity of the Church taught that 'outside the church there is no salvation'. He was beheaded under Valerian.
people/cyprian/keyIdeas/0: Unity of the church in the episcopate
people/novatian/summary: A Roman presbyter and author of the first major Latin treatise On the Trinity. After Cornelius was elected bishop and favoured readmitting the lapsed, Novatian was consecrated rival bishop, founding a rigorist church that lasted for centuries. He may have died a martyr under Valerian.
people/sabellius/summary: A third-century teacher in Rome (fl. c. 215) condemned by Pope Callistus. Little survives of his own words; opponents describe him as teaching that Father, Son and Spirit are successive modes or names of one divine person. 'Sabellianism' became the standard label for modalism.
people/sabellius/keyIdeas/0: Modalism: one God revealed in three modes
people/paul-of-samosata/summary: Bishop of Antioch and an official of Queen Zenobia of Palmyra, deposed by a synod in 268 for teaching that Jesus was a man inspired by the divine Word rather than the Word incarnate. He is regarded as a representative of dynamic monarchianism or adoptionism.
people/paul-of-samosata/keyIdeas/1: Rejection of a personal pre-existent Son
